In order to generate a finite element model, one needs to know or make informed 1051 assumptions to define appropriate geometric (i.e., anatomy and shape), material property (e.g., 1052 Neo-Hookean parameters), and boundary/loading conditions (i.e., how different parts/tissues 1053 interact with one another and their environment). The goal of the forward finite element method is 1054 to simulate specific tissues in order to predict resulting stresses and strains during a certain 1055 scenario—for example, simulating LA stresses and/or strains during vaginal delivery. For the 1056 reverse finite element method, the goal is to use known forces and displacements to calculate the 1057 tissues material properties. 1058 It is expected that computational simulations will be able to determine how injuries to the 1059 pelvic floor muscles, pelvic connective tissues, perineum, and the urethral and anal sphincters, 1060 may contribute to the development of PFDs. This has already been mentioned in this chapter, but it 1168 should again be emphasized. There is a significant time delay between vaginal birth and the onset 1169 of pelvic floor disorder symptoms. While improvements in imaging, understanding tissue damage, 1170 and computational modeling will help us to uncover more details about the impact of vaginal 1171 childbirth, creating preventative strategies necessitates that we understand the mechanisms that 1172 relate birth injury with the onset of symptoms. It is very likely that pregnancy and delivery disrupt 1173 mechano-homeostasis and leads to degradative changes in other supporting tissues that take time 1174 to manifest. This process is likely exacerbated by changes in hormones, weight gain, and other 1175 factors that impact how forces are being transferred within the pelvis (e.g. repetitive heavy lifting, 1176 chronic straining). 1177 In terms of computational research, we need to work to improve model validation and 1178 application. Simulations of vaginal delivery, for example, should ideally be able to mimic the 1179 vaginal delivery of specific patients. However, we should also avoid the pitfall of having models 1180 be so specific that they can only be reasonably applied to a few individuals. By utilizing diverse 1181 patient populations in model development and performing robust studies when determining 1182 appropriate model inputs (such as material properties, geometry/anatomy, and boundary/loading 1183 conditions), this issue can be overcome. In this chapter, we present an overview of the effects of estrogen and other hormones 39 on the pelvic floor structure and function and summarise major gaps in the current literature. 40 41 Molecular mechanisms of estrogen action 42 The term “estrogens” refers to a group of primary female sex hormones. There are four 43 forms of estrogens: Estrone (E1), Estradiol (E2), Estriol (E3) and Estretrol (E4)2. Chemically, 44 estrogens belong to the family of organic compounds known as steroids. In women, estrogens are 45 primarily synthesized in the granulosa and theca cells of the ovaries, but also in smaller amounts 46 by other tissues such as liver, pancreas, adrenal glands, adipose tissue, breast and placenta during 47 pregnancy. 48 E2 (17β-estradiol) is the most common and potent form of estrogen during female 49 reproductive years. 3 It plays an important role in the development of reproductive system and 50 secondary sexual characteristics during puberty.4,5,6 While females produce all estrogens 51 throughout life, E3 and E4 are predominantly found during pregnancy, and E1 is usually present 52 at higher levels during menopause.7 The main source of E2 biosynthesis is dietary cholesterol. E2 53 is synthesised due to activity of multiple enzymes, the most important of which are aromatase 54 (CYP19A1) and 17β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (17-HSD). Aromatase is widely distributed 55 in gonadal and extra-gonadal tissues including the bone, brain, adipose tissue, and blood vessels 8. 56 E1 that is mainly produced during menopause in peripheral extra-gonadal tissues, can be 57 transformed to E2 by the 17-HSD enzyme in adipose and breast tissue, vascular endothelium, 58 smooth muscle cells, brain and bone cells, where it is metabolized.9 The bioactivity and levels of 59 circulating estrogens is controlled by gonadotropins (FSH and LH) via hypothalamic-pituitary 60 feedback. In humans, the bioavailability of estrogens is restricted by high-affinity binding to 61 circulating sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG). 10 Only 1–5% of circulating E2 (the free 2 62 fraction that is not bound to SHBG, albumin, or other proteins) is thought to be biologically 63 active.11 64 65 Molecular mechanism of estrogen action in the female pelvic floor and genitourinary tract 66 At the cellular level, E2 mediates its genomic actions by binding to their specific nuclear 67 receptors and effecting the expression of target genes. In the female pelvis, estrogen receptors 68 (ERs) are found in the female squamous epithelium of the proximal and distal urethra, vagina, 69 trigone of the bladder, and anal canal. Furthermore, they are expressed in the para-urethral tissues, 70 urethral sphincter, uterosacral ligaments and pelvic floor musculature.12 Two distinct estrogen 71 receptors are described in the literature - alpha (ERα) and beta (ERβ). Both act as the ligand- 72 activated transcription factors, which are variably expressed in different tissues.13,14,15,16 Each is 73 coded by its own gene (ESR1 and ESR2, respectively), and requires homodimerization, where two 74 identical proteins are combined, before binding its ligand or to specific DNA sequences called 75 estrogen response elements (EREs). In addition to the full-length ERα isoform (66kDa), several 76 shorter isoforms (36kDa, 46kDa) have been identified as a result of the presence of alternate start 77 codons, or as products of alternative splicing. ERβ also exists in 5 distinct isoforms, ERβ1-5.17 78 The shorter isoforms cannot activate transcription. Instead, they form heterodimers with the full- 79 length ERα and inhibit its control of transcriptional activity. Mechanism of genomic signalling is 80 determined by E2 liganding to ERα and ERβ, which regulate expression of specific genes either 81 directly through ERE sites in gene promoters in the nucleus of target cells (Figure 1) or indirectly 82 by binding with and modulating the activity of other transcription factors (i.e. NFkB).18 ERs act 83 through direct binding to EREs to initiate gene expression or to non-EREs by binding other 84 transcription factors, such as Activator Protein-1 (AP1) or Specificity Protein-1 (SP-1). In the 85 absence of ligand, the ER homodimers recruit a complex of factors (co-repressors) that repress 86 transcription and co-activators to promote transcription. Historically, the 571 impact of obesity on the female pelvic floor has been assumed to be simply mechanical in nature. 572 Here we seek to examine the current literature describing the more intricate role of obesity and 573 associated chronic inflammation and oxidative stress, metabolic syndrome, insulin resistance and 574 diabetes and the overlap of these conditions with hormonal imbalances in androgens, thyroid 575 hormones and vitamin D. Our goal is not only to review the literature, but also integrate the existing 576 body of knowledge in a way conducive to the identification of critical gaps that should fuel novel 577 investigations. 578 579 Androgens 580 Although relatively less studied, androgens also vary in women during their lifetime. 581 Consequently, these hormones may play a putative role in PFDs, the incidence of which increases 582 with menopause. Androgens have established roles in skeletal muscle strength, bone density, and 583 connective tissue integrity in other systems, but their role in the female pelvic floor has not been 584 well characterized. 25 585 Androgens, typically thought of as “male” hormones, are present in women in significant 586 levels throughout the reproductive lifespan. Androgen production is initiated in the ovaries and the 587 adrenal glands in response to luteinizing hormone (LH) and adrenocorticotrophic hormone 588 (ACTH). The major androgens produced are testosterone, androstenedione, and 589 dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA), all of which are cholesterol derivatives. In the ovary, cholesterol 590 is first converted to DHEA and then to androstenedione and testosterone, contributing to plasma 591 testosterone levels directly and indirectly via peripheral conversion of circulating androstenedione. 592 The adrenal glands contribute to circulating levels of DHEA and ultimately DHEA sulfate (DHEA- 593 S) that is derived from DHEA, and testosterone. Circulating testosterone is present in multiple 594 forms: free (1-2%), bound to sex hormone binding globulin (SHBG) (~66%), and loosely bound 595 to albumin (~31%).216, 217 Loosely bound and free testosterone are bioavailable, in contrast, bound 596 testosterone has diminished biological activity. Consequently, the level of SHBG (produced by the 597 liver) can alter the amount of bioavailable testosterone. Circulating levels of SHBG increase with 598 increased circulating estrogen levels. Circulating testosterone levels can also be diminished by 599 aromatization to estradiol, which occurs in the ovary and peripherally. Circulating testosterone can 600 also be converted by 5α-reductase to the potent androgen - dihydrotestosterone (DHT). More 601 recently identified circulating androgens that are synthesized peripherally include 11- 602 ketoandrostenedione (11KA), 11-ketotestosterone (11KHT), and 11-ketodihydrotestosterone 603 (11KDH).216 These 11-oxygenated C19 steroids possess similar androgenic potency to 604 testosterone and DHT and can bind and activate androgen receptors in men.216 The complexity of 605 androgen signaling and difficulty in measuring lower circulating levels of androgens in females 606 have made the characterization and quantification of these hormones in women more challenging. 607 During the lifespan of a woman, the concentration of circulating androgens changes 608 significantly. A cross-sectional study of 588 premenopausal women ages 18-39 characterized 609 androgen levels across the menstrual cycle. Testosterone and androstenedione are lowest in the 610 early follicular phase and are higher in the midcycle and luteal phases.216 In contrast, DHEA, 611 11KA, and 11KT were unchanged during the menstrual cycle. Mechanistic studies in murine models have begun to characterize the role of androgens in 624 the pelvic floor. In male rats, pelvic skeletal muscles, including levator ani and external urethral 625 sphincter, are androgen sensitive as evident by levator ani atrophy in response to androgen removal 626 by gonadectomy.158 Similarly, ovariectomized female rats exhibit levator ani atrophy. 627 Interestingly, this atrophy can be rescued by selective androgen receptor modulators, suggesting 628 that ovarian testosterone rather than estrogen may be needed for preservation of levator ani muscle 629 mass.159 Functional improvement in PFDs with androgen treatment has also been demonstrated in 630 the rat model. In the sciatic nerve transection female rat model of SUI, leak point pressures return 631 to control values with testosterone treatment.160 632 Despite paucity of studies, these findings suggest that androgen receptors are present in 633 the female pelvic floor and may be needed to maintain muscle mass and function. Additional 634 research is needed to clarify the role of androgens in the pathogenesis and potential treatment of 635 PFDs. Detailed characterization of specific androgen levels using high sensitivity quantitative 636 testing, such as mass spectroscopy-based analysis, is needed to accurately characterize the 637 relationship of androgens with PFDs. In addition, more animal studies are needed to establish a 638 mechanistic link between specific androgens and the function of the integral components of the 639 female pelvic floor. Furthermore, long-term safety and efficacy studies of androgen regimens in 640 women are needed to inform clinical practice and select appropriate patient populations for 641 potential treatments. Topical DHEA vaginal preparations and systemic androgen therapies are 642 clinically utilized to improve sexual health in women. We do not know what impact, if any, these 643 treatments have on the development, progression, or resolution of PFDs long-term. 644 645 Vitamin D 27 646 Vitamin D is a fat-soluble steroid hormone that is integral for the regulation of calcium 647 homeostasis in bone and skeletal muscle. Vitamin D is predominantly produced in the skin, where 648 provitamin D (7-dehydrocholesterol) is converted to cholecalciferol (D3) by ultraviolet B rays. 649 Circulating D3 then binds to vitamin D binding protein (VDBP) and can be metabolized to 25- 650 hydroxyvitamin D2 [25(OH)D]. In the kidney 25(OH)D2 is converted to active metabolite calcitriol 651 [1,25 (OH)D2]. The production of these derivatives is closely coupled to calcium homeostasis and 652 is regulated by calcium, phosphorous and parathyroid hormone. 653 Vitamin D insufficiency and deficiency are common, affecting approximately 75% of 654 both older (>65) adults and reproductive age women.161,162,163 Multiple demographic and 655 socioeconomic factors have been associated with vitamin D deficiency, including female sex, 656 obesity, African American race, and low income. 164,165 Most literature has focused on the adverse 657 impact of vitamin D deficiency on the skeleton and appendicular muscles; however, a body of 658 literature investigating the relationship between vitamin D and PFDs is growing. 659 Epidemiologic studies examining the relationship between vitamin D and PFDs, such as 660 large cross-sectional analysis 161 of 1881 non-pregnant women enrolled in the National Health and 661 Nutrition Examination Survey, determined that vitamin D levels are significantly lower in women 662 with at least one reported PFD compared to women without self-reported PFDs, regardless of age. 663 In a retrospective study of 394 women with the preponderance of postmenopausal Caucasian 664 participants, mean vitamin D levels were higher in women without compared to with symptomatic 665 PFDs, with worse incontinence impact questionnaire scores associated with vitamin D 666 insufficiency.166 Overall, the epidemiologic literature suggests that decreased vitamin D levels 667 coincide with the presence of PFDs independent of age. Addressing these gaps may open novel avenues of 67 therapeutic interventions in management of POP and SUI with the ultimate goal of improving 68 women’s health. 69 70 Introduction 71 POP and SUI, while two distinct conditions, share risk factors and hence, their 72 pathophysiologic bases are likely similar. Both substantially negatively impact quality of life and 73 mental health of affected individuals and thus, incur substantial cost to the livelihood of women 74 world-wide. These conditions are common, impacting roughly 30-50% of the female population 75 over the age of 50 years and incur a lifetime risk of undergoing a single surgical procedure to repair 76 either POP or SUI of 20% by age 80 (1). In the United States, the separate cumulative risk for 77 POP surgery is 12.6% and for SUI surgery 13.6%, with societal costs estimated to exceed $10 78 billion annually (2-5). A significantly higher number of women seek non-surgical or conservative 79 treatment options, also with significant associated costs. Despite the high prevalence of POP and 80 SUI, the frequent need for surgical intervention, associated costs, and the substantial impact upon 81 quality of life, the natural history and underlying mechanisms of these pelvic floor disorders 82 (PFDs), and especially POP, remain poorly understood. 83 The predominant risk factor for both SUI and POP is vaginal delivery. Additional risks 84 include age, menopause, obesity, and race (6-11). Among these additional risks, age is perhaps the 85 most impactful. Women above the age of 50 represent the majority of patients presenting for 86 management of clinically significant POP (12). The prevalence of SUI peaks in the 5th decade and 87 the prevalence of mixed incontinence, which includes SUI and urge urinary incontinence, 88 dramatically increases with age thereafter, resulting in a disproportionate number of women 89 seeking care for their incontinence after age 60 (8, 13). As the population over 65 is forecasted to 90 increase to 88.5 million by 2050, and as 55% of those 65 and older will be female (11), the human 91 and economic impact of POP and SUI is expected to rise substantially. Thus, improving our 92 understanding of aging as a risk factor for POP and SUI is imperative if preventative measures are 93 to be developed. 94 Aging is a multifaceted process associated with an overall functional decline spanning 95 nearly all tissue and organ systems including those in the pelvis, and is a significant risk factor for 96 many diseases and conditions (14). Aging has been well investigated in the context of major 97 conditions including cancer, and cardiovascular and neurodegenerative diseases. Mechanistic 98 investigations of the impacts of aging at the cellular level in these conditions have led to the 99 identification of nine suggested “hallmarks” of aging (14). These hallmarks manifest during the 100 degenerative processes of aging and include genomic instability, telomere attrition, epigenetic 101 alterations, loss of proteostasis, deregulated nutrient sensing, mitochondrial dysfunction, cellular 102 senescence, stem cell exhaustion, and altered intercellular communication (14). These hallmarks 103 provide a framework for the study of the impact of mechanisms of aging on degenerative 104 processes. Investigations of aging at the cellular level have led to significant improvements in the 105 understanding and treatment of many prevalent age-related disease processes. However, despite 106 the known increases in the incidence of POP and incontinence with aging, there have been few 107 mechanistic studies into the role of aging in the processes which underlie POP and SUI. 108 Furthermore, a key aspect of aging, namely the immune changes that occur with age, termed 109 inflammaging or immunosenescence, have not been investigated in depth in the pathogenesis of 110 POP or SUI and will be explored here. 111 The pathophysiology of POP and SUI can be broadly attributed to deterioration in the 112 structure and function of the vagina and urethra, respectively, and the soft tissues that support 113 them. While initial injury may be damage to nerves, connective tisues, and muscles at childbirth, 114 additional decompensation occurs mostly from aging and age-related diseases over time. The 115 primary structures involved in support of the pelvic organs are the pelvic floor muscles (PFMs) 116 and supportive connective tissues (reviewed in (15)). The vagina is comprised of a stratified 117 squamous epithelium followed by a dense connective tissue enriched with collagen and elastin and 118 a bilayer of smooth muscle. The urethra is supported by the periurethral ligaments, the pelvic 119 diaphragm, and the levator ani muscles. It is comprised of a stratified squamous epithelium, a 120 spongy submucosa, a middle smooth muscle layer, and an outer fibroelastic layer. Urethral closure 121 is achieved via active and passive mechanisms (13, 16, 17). At rest, the urethra is closed by 122 submucosal vessels, elastin and connective tissue, smooth muscle and neural networks. A 123 voluntary striated sphincter muscle forms the outermost layer that is highly interactive with the 124 levator ani muscles. During increases in intra-abdominal pressure, levator ani and the supportive 125 connective tissues interact in a highly orchestrated fashion to maintain the pelvic organs, such as 126 the vagina and the urethra, in their normal anatomic position. 127 128 Changes in Cellular Function with POP and SUI in Aging 129 While each of the hallmarks of aging described above have been shown to have distinct 130 impact upon cellular behavior, the overall result of these changes is generally referred to as cellular 131 senescence (14). Cellular senescence is characterized by cell cycle arrest and a senescence 132 associated secretory phenotype (SASP) (14, 18, 19). SASP positive senescent cells accumulate 133 over the life span in rodents, primates, and humans, and are more often found in renewable tissues 134 and sites of chronic inflammation (19, 20). SASP cells have also been shown to be present in 135 settings characterized by trauma or excess loading such as posttraumatic osteoarthritis (21, 22). 136 The most common cell-intrinsic change resulting in a senescent phenotype is the accumulation of 137 genetic changes within cells over the course of a lifetime. Such changes are continually occurring 138 due to exogenous physical and chemical challenges, DNA replication errors, and exposure to 139 oxidative stress resulting in a diverse range of point mutations, translocations, chromosomal gains 140 and losses, and telomere shortening. The ensuing changes can occur in the nuclear DNA as well 141 as mitochondrial DNA, resulting in a range of dysfunctional outcomes, including alteration of 142 essential gene and transcriptional mechanisms as well as functional phenotypes. Certain regions 143 of the DNA are more susceptible to age-related modifications (23). For example, it is well 144 established that telomere shortening occurs with aging (20, 23), eventually leading to the 145 progressive loss of proliferative capacity of cells known as the Hayflick limit (24). Each of these 146 changes can lead to dysregulation of tissue homeostasis and SASP phenotype. A recent review by 147 Huang, et al, examined multiple aspects of cellular senescence and their relationship to POP, 148 suggesting a role for senescence of fibroblasts in the pathogenesis of POP (25). However, POP- 149 specific studies of cellular senescence are few and the exact implications of how the observed 150 cellular changes contribute to POP and SUI pathogenesis remains an important avenue for 151 investigation. Microarray studies of the pubococcygeus muscle as well as uterosacral and round 153 ligaments, have suggested that there are differences in gene expression associated with SUI and 154 POP (26, 27). These studies, as well as a recent systematic review examining both specific gene 155 and whole genome/proteome level data sets demonstrate that genes associated with extracellular 156 matrix (ECM) production and maintenance, estrogen receptors, inflammatory mediators, as well 157 as structural proteins related to actin and myosin are altered in patients with POP (26-30). 158 However, the degree to which these expression profiles are induced by age-related changes versus 159 hereditary- or injury-induced mechanisms remains an open question. 160 161 Cellular Dysfunction in POP and Aging 162 Age-related mitochondrial dysfunction is a well-known component of the aging process 163 (14, 31). The mitochondrial free radical theory of aging suggests that progressive mitochondrial 164 dysfunction leads to increased production of reactive oxygen species (32), resulting in further 165 cellular, mitochondrial, and tissue level damage as well as dysfunction in cellular bioenergetics 166 (energy production, expenditure); however others suggest that oxidative stress is only one of many 167 mechanisms which underlie aging and cellular dysfunction (14, 33). Studies of mitochondrial 168 dysfunction in postmenopausal women with POP have shown that fibroblasts isolated from the 169 uterosacral ligaments of patients with POP were associated with slower proliferation, reduced 170 viability and increased expression of mitofusin 2 (Mfn2), an outer mitochondrial membrane 171 GTPase critical for mitochondrial fusion, as well as downregulated expression of procollagen. 172 These data suggest a link between mitochondrial function and collagen production as the increased 173 expression level of Mfn2 could inhibit the proliferation and cell cycle of fibroblasts by mediating 174 Ras/Raf/ERK pathway, leading to the decrease in collagen synthesis and eventually tissue 175 degradation (34). Another study examined the prevalence of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) 176 changes in the uterosacral ligaments, showing that depletion of mtDNA, including rearrangements 177 of mtDNA4977, were accumulated in the uterosacral ligaments of women with POP, especially 178 those with stages III and IV (35). mtDNA4977 is among the most common mtDNA variations 179 found in aging human tissues (36). This deletion is also associated with increased oxidative stress 180 within aging tissues’ environment, suggesting POP may be linked to oxidative damage. The 181 negative impact of aging on the function of mitochondria in the urethra and its supportive tissues 182 is less clear. Elucidation of the mechanisms underpinning this process might provide novel 183 avenues for therapeutic interventions to manage POP. 184 Oxidative stress has been suggested as a primary driver of the genetic changes observed 185 with aging. Increases in oxidative stress are known to occur over the lifespan, potentially due to 186 concurrent decreases in the production and function of oxidative stress regulating molecules such 187 as superoxide dismutase. In the context of POP, Kim, et al., demonstrated that indicators of 188 oxidative stress were increased in the uterosacral ligaments of women with prolapse (meanSD 189 age 55.59.0 years) compared to age matched controls (meanSD age 54.98.4 years), as 190 evidenced by the increased expression of 8-OHdG and 4-hrdroxy-2-nonenal identified by 191 immunohistochemistry (37). Additional analysis demonstrated that women with stage III and IV 192 prolapse also demonstrate evidence of mitochondrial apoptosis (37). In vitro studies have 193 demonstrated that mechanical strain can induce cellular oxidative stress via the PI3K/Akt pathway, 194 leading to apoptosis and senescence of human uterosacral ligament fibroblasts (38, 39). Further 195 investigation showed that oxidative stress also induced a shift towards collagen catabolism, 196 reduced collagen I production, and increased matrix metalloproteinase (MMP) expression in 197 human uterosacral ligament fibroblasts (38, 39). The epigenome includes alterations that are defined as reversible heritable 227 changes to the genome that do not involve changes in the DNA sequence. The mechanisms 228 responsible for these changes include alterations in DNA methylation patterns, posttranslational 229 modification of histones, chromatin remodeling, and non-coding microRNAs (miRNA) (50). 230 These epigenetic modifications have been identified as one of the hallmark mechanisms of aging, 231 and are thought to potentially explain the diverse patterns of physical decline within the population 232 (14, 49, 51-53). Epigenetic mechanisms may also play a role in the compromise of the pelvic 233 support system. Since aging is a risk factor for POP and urinary incontinence, epigenetic 234 mechanisms could explain how aging affects the deterioration of the tissues providing support to 235 the pelvic organs including the vagina and urethra. 236 Longevity studies have demonstrated that genetic factors explain 20-30% of the differences 237 observed in the lifespans of monozygotic twins, and that epigenetic drift accumulated during their 238 lifetime was responsible for the remaining differences (54-57). Similarly, in a twin study 239 conducted by Altman et al., 3,376 mono- and 5,067 di-zygotic female twin pairs were identified 240 from the Swedish Twin Registry and their records were cross-linked to the Swedish Inpatient 241 Registry that contains data on individual hospital discharges to determine the genetic and 242 environmental influence on the incidence of SUI and POP surgery. Using statistical modeling, it 243 was determined that genetic and non-shared environmental factors equally contribute ~40% of the 244 variation in risk for the development of POP and SUI, however, the interrelationship between 245 genetics and the environment remain unknown (58). Investigating the influence of environmental 246 factors and epigenetic regulation of genes is promising to close this gap in knowledge. Clear links have been established between cellular dysfunction and tissue 489 degradation, including the progressive changes in ECM content and structure seen in POP and 490 SUI. However, tissue resident fibroblasts and muscle cells are not the only populations which 491 participate in the pathogenesis of these conditions. Aging is also well known to affect the immune 492 cells of both the innate and adaptive immune systems. These changes are likely to have significant 493 impact both on the pathogenesis of POP/SUI as well as the ability to treat using surgical 494 interventions. 495 Immunosenescence is a phenomenon occurring with advanced age and has been associated 496 with increase susceptibility to infection, autoimmune disorders, and cancer related mortality (113- 497 115). While the definition of senescence usually includes the arrest of cell division, such as that 498 discussed above for fibroblasts (Hayflick limit), immunosenescence is better characterized by a 499 reduction in circulating cells, delayed migration to sites of injury, and dysregulated immune 500 responses (115, 116). Immunosenescence, much like cellular senescence, is characterized by 501 increased systemic levels of inflammatory cytokines and oxidative species (117, 118). This 502 process has been referred to as “inflammaging” as the effects of this elevated systemic cytokine 503 milieu and resultant oxidative stress can cause tissue

disorders, and cancer related mortality (113- 497 115). Immunosenescence, much like cellular senescence, is characterized by 501 increased systemic levels of inflammatory cytokines and oxidative species (117, 118). This 502 process has been referred to as “inflammaging” as the effects of this elevated systemic cytokine 503 milieu and resultant oxidative stress can cause tissue damage and senescence of stromal cells, 504 resulting in their acquisition of the SASP (19, 118). 505 The role of innate immune system in the female pelvic floor and genitourinary tract is 506 detailed in the The Impact of Hormonal Milieu on the Female Pelvic Floor Structure and Function. 507 The innate immune system includes neutrophils, eosinophils, basophil, mast cells, innate lymphoid 508 cells, and antigen presenting cells. Each of these cells provides a coordinated response which 509 ideally results in the restoration of tissue homeostasis (119). Multiple defects in this response have 510 been observed in aging. For example, dendritic cell activation is impaired in aging, resulting in 511 impaired ability to cross tissue barriers, and to elicit responses from the adaptive immune system 512 (120, 121). Similarly, monocytes and macrophages, which have recently been shown to be key 513 mediators of tissue homeostasis, wound healing, and the response to implanted materials, are 514 altered over the lifespan (122, 123). Macrophages have been shown to accumulate in multiple 515 tissues including the liver, heart and adipose tissues with age (115, 124, 125). Accumulation has 516 also recently been observed in the reproductive system with aging, corresponding with fibrosis in 517 the stroma of the ovary (126); and in aging bladders (127, 128). Of note, though multiple studies 518 have shown increases in inflammatory mediators in patients with prolapse, studies of uterosacral 519 and round ligaments of women undergoing hysterectomy for POP were not found to have 520 increased inflammatory infiltrates as compared to controls (26). 521 Macrophage recruitment is delayed in aging, and a reduction in major histocompatibility 522 complex II has been observed, leading to reduced antigen presentation and cross talk with the 523 adaptive immune system (129, 130). Further, a reduction in the ability of macrophages to polarize 524 towards M1, pro-inflammatory, and M2 anti-inflammatory, homeostatic phenotypes has been 525 observed (131). Reductions in macrophage function have been correlated with increased incidence 526 of infections with age, particularly in postmenopausal women. This dysregulation in the innate 527 immune response is associated with slow and incomplete wound healing as well as the loss of 528 tissue homeostasis with aging and has been implicated in a wide range of age-related diseases. 529 Recent studies of 12 women (mean age 57.21±12.11) have taken bioinformatics approaches to 530 identify immune changes in POP and identified mast cells and neutrophils infiltration to be higher 531 in POP tissues (132). In addition, inflammatory cytokines and genes associated with cytokine- 532 cytokine-receptor interactions and chemokine signaling pathways have been implicated in POP. 533 Few studies have identified immunologic changes in women with SUI. However, one recent study 534 utilized genome-wide association to study 8,979 European women with stress incontinence, 535 urgency incontinence, and all incontinence phenotpyes (133). The results identified and confirmed 536 two signle nucleotide polymorphisms, endothelin 1 (EDN1) and macrophage receptor with 537 collagenous structure (MARCO) to be associated with urgency incontinence and stress 538 incontinence, respectively. These findings suggest a potential role for the innate immune response 539 in stress urinary incontinence, possibly due to persistent bacterial coonization in lower urinary tract 540 system. However, significant work is needed to demonstrate and elucidate the role of the innate 541 immune system in SUI. 542 Adaptive immune cells, which include T cell and B cell types could also play a role in POP 543 and SUI. However, little is known regarding these populations in the aging pelvic floor. Vaginal estrogen has shown efficacy in improving age associated adaptive immune 549 changes in reconstructive surgery for pelvic organ prolapse (134). Surgical interventions naturally elicit a 558 wound healing response. Wound healing is a highly dynamic process characterized by a series of 559 overlapping events orchestrated by numerous resident and recruited immune cells, soluble factors, 560 and matrix assembly (136, 137). Immediately following injury, a rapid inflammatory response 561 ensues with the initiation of the innate immune response (138, 139). Resident dendritic cells and 562 monocytes release cytokines to facilitate migration and differentiation of macrophages, at the site 563 of injury. Macrophages are a key mediator of the wound healing process, and dysregulation of 564 their phenotypes results in delayed or deficient wound healing (138, 139) . This is followed by 565 the deposition of extracellular matrix and subsequent remodeling with resolution of the wound 566 healing process or scarring as an outcome. This series of events occurs following tissue injury, 567 regardless of the cause, including those caused by vaginal delivery or surgical intervention, for 568 example. 569 Prosthetic mesh materials are commonly used in the repair of POP to provide mechanical 570 support to the pelvic floor and to reduce recurrence rates (140-142). While mesh implantation has 571 been shown to improve anatomical outcomes in the anterior and apical compartments, 572 complications associated with mesh usage are observed (143-146). These include mesh exposure 573 through the vaginal wall, shrinkage, erosion and pain. Recent work has shown that these 574 complications may be attributable, at least in part, to the host immune response following 575 implantation (102, 103). Chronic activation of the M1, pro-inflammatory macrophage response 576 has been associated with erosion, while chronic activation of a more M2, pro-healing, phenotype 577 has been associated with fibrosis and pain (102). Thus, careful orchestration of the macrophage 578 response to implantable mesh materials is required for integration and long-term success. Multiple 579 studies have now demonstrated that mesh materials which elicit stronger M1 type responses are 580 associated with increased vaginal tissue degradation following implantation in primate studies 581 (103, 135, 147-149). Others have shown that methods which shift the early host response towards 582 an M2 phenotype are associated with improved integration and remodeling outcomes (150-152). 583 While age-related defects in the wound healing process have not been clearly tied to the 584 pathogenesis of POP, they may play an important role in the success or failure of surgical 585 reconstruction or the outcome of prosthetic mesh implantation. A recent study investigated age- 586 associated differences in macrophage response in a rodent model of vaginal wound healing (153). 587 Histological analysis showed clear differences in wound healing, with more rapid wound closure 588 in young rats (12 weeks old) as compared to aged rats (12 months old). The aged rats also exhibited 589 a more robust and sustained macrophage response characterized by increased TNF- (Tumor 590 Necrosis Factor alpha) and iNOS (inducible Nitric Oxide Synthase) expression and an increased 591 ratio of M1:M2 immunolabeled macrophages within the wound site than was observed in young 592 animals. Additional studies in this rat model demonstrated that these changes in the host response 593 were correlated with expression of macrophage-migration inhibitory growth factor within the site 594 of tissue remodeling and resulted in lower tensile strength of tissues at 30 days post injury (154). 595 Recent studies have further examined variations in the host response to implanted materials 596 with increasing age (150, 155). For example, one study examined the host response to 597 polypropylene mesh in an aged rodent model (155). These studies showed a delayed macrophage 598 response as well as dysregulation of macrophage polarization with a chronic increase in the M1 599 phenotype in aged (18 months) animals. The study further examined the circulating macrophage 600 population, showing that the ability of the cells to migrate and switch polarization states was 601 largely intact, suggesting that the local tissue environment may have been responsible for the 602

As each of these hallmarks of aging is interrelated, 615 significant mechanistic work is needed to demonstrate that the observed changes are related to cell 616 intrinsic dysfunction, cell cell communication, epigenetic changes, and how the observed changes 617 affect both cellular behavior, proteostasis, nutrient sensingas well as overall tissue structure and 618 function leading to pelvic floor dysfunction. Impact of recruitment of stromal cells and immune 619 cells, stem cell exhaustion and other changes to the tissue environment upon the pathogenesis of 620 POP and SUI needs to be determined. Immunological underpinnings driving pathogenesis of 621 POP/SUI and implicated in mesh repair remain an important and highly understudied aspect of 622 understanding of POP and SUI mechanisms and clinical management. Role for innate immunity 623 and adaptive immunity are beginning to be identified along with immune signatures of POP and 624 SUI. Better understanding of types of immune cell infiltrates, timing and dynamics of infiltration, 625 and impact on pelvic floor homeostasis, injury, and repair in this tissue is needed for limiting 626 adverse conditions with mesh replacement and other interventions. Thus, these are areas of 627 research that has many opportunities for advancement of the field of Female Pelvic Medicine and 628 Reconstructive Pelvic Surgery since a better understanding of the role of aging in POP and SUI 629 will rationally lead to an improved ability to prevent or treat these conditions.. 630 631 632 Knowledge Gaps 633 Aging is a clear risk factor for POP and SUI. However, the mechanisms which lead to the 634 pathogenesis of these conditions are not well elucidated. Evidence exists to suggest that the 635 pathogenesis of POP and SUI is tied to age-related changes in cellular function, leading to 636 imbalanced proteostasis, and resulting in degradative changes at the tissue level. However, while 637 such mechanisms have been well studied in other tissues and organs as well as in many age-related 638 disease processes, they remain under-investigated in the pelvic floor and in the setting of POP and 639 SUI. Understanding the mechanism of age-related changes in the pelvic floor will logically lead 640 to improved ability to manage or prevent POP.
